To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
chromium(III) is released from leather under acidic conditions, whereas chromium(VI) is released under basic conditions.
chromium(III) can be released in a significant amount from leather products under certain conditions, and this release can be prevented by using appropriate tanning processes.

the Cr(VI) content in the leather samples was in the range of 0.1–0.4 mg kg −1, the total Cr content was in the range 1.1–1.7 mg kg −1 (with a median of 1.5), and the total Cr content is approximately 1.2% of the total Cr content.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a method to measure Cr(VI) and Cr(III) in leather and the evaluation of the release of Cr(VI) from leather products in contact with skin.
the release of Cr(III) and Cr(VI) from leather products under different conditions of exposure, and with the identification of the main factors that control Cr(VI) release.
the development of a new method for the determination of the total chromium content in leather products and its implementation in the leather industry.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
chromium is a carcinogen.
the use of tanning agents based on chromium(III) compounds does not pose any health risks.
leather products, which are not intended to be in contact with the skin, should not contain more than 3 mg Cr/kg.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the release of Cr(VI) from leather is a complex phenomenon that is dependent on many factors, such as pH and ionic strength.
the release of Cr(VI) from leather is a function of the leather pH, the pH of the solution, the temperature and the time of contact.
the chromium released from the leather depends on the pH, the temperature and the contact time with the solution.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Cr(III) is the predominant form released from tanned leather, and Cr(VI) is not released in significant amounts.
the release of Cr(VI) is not a function of the leather’s chromium content, but of the leather’s pH.
the Cr release from leather products can be significantly reduced by using a Cr(III)-containing leather tanning process.
